clue.text: A group of detectives in charge is sharp

blocks.note: taken as written
the Criminal Investigation Department, the British police detective branch
i/c is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A squad of detectives with a boss in charge is said to be on the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: An acidic remark or taste is tart and cutting, so the adjective is a synonym of sharp.

clue.text: Charlie needing a leg to get up?

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a leg is one example of a limb

explanation.surface: Someone called Charlie asks for a leg-up to get on a horse or over a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: To climb is to go up or ascend, so get up in the sense of mounting is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Carts maid off in highly emotional scenes

indicators.note: something gone off has gone wrong or awry, so its letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A servant drags someone away amid tearful, emotional goings-on.
explanation.definitionFit: Dramatics means exaggerated, theatrical behaviour, a display of over-the-top emotion.

clue.text: Quite theatrical MC irritated with pay

indicators.note: irritated suggests being stirred up, so the letters are mixed around

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A flamboyant master of ceremonies gets cross about his fee.
explanation.definitionFit: Campy describes an affected, exaggerated, showy style, so it is a fair match for somewhat theatrical.

clue.text: Concerning and a little bit far away

blocks.note: re is the Latin-derived word for about or concerning
a mote is a speck or tiny particle

explanation.surface: Something is described as a tiny bit distant, with a fussy 'concerning' thrown in.
explanation.definitionFit: A remote place is distant from everything else, so the adjective is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Cad meets obstruction in European city

blocks.note: a rotter is a dated British term for a scoundrel
a dam blocks a river

explanation.surface: A scoundrel runs into a roadblock somewhere on the Continent.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotterdam is a major port city in the Netherlands, so it is one example of a city in Europe.

clue.text: Set up a machine to make money

indicators.note: in a down answer, setting something up turns it to read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a loom is a weaving machine

explanation.surface: Advice to install a machine as a way of earning cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Moola is a slang term for cash, a synonym for money.

clue.text: The Yorkshire artist making a bride's wedding gear?

blocks.note: in Yorkshire dialect the is shortened to t'
Henri Rousseau, the French painter

explanation.surface: A northern painter is pictured designing a bride's outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: A trousseau is the clothes and linen a bride gathers for her marriage.

clue.text: Lightened up about weight, seeing fold of loose skin

indicators.note: in a down answer, up means the word for lightened is read from the bottom
about means going around, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: to pale is to grow lighter in colour
W is the abbreviation for weight

explanation.surface: Someone cheered up about their weight on seeing a sagging fold of skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lightened up' reads as cheered up, but it is PALED turned round, giving DELAP around W.
explanation.definitionFit: A dewlap is the loose fold of skin hanging from the throat of cattle and some other animals.

clue.text: More colourful, whichever way you look at it

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: whichever way the solver reads the word, forwards or back, it comes out the same

blocks.note: this comparative reads identically in both directions

explanation.surface: Something is declared more vivid from every angle.
explanation.definitionFit: Redder is the comparative of red, a shade more intense in hue, so a fair sense of more colourful.

clue.text: Heather is another girl's name

blocks.note: first meaning: the botanical genus of heathers
second meaning: a female first name, as Heather itself is

explanation.surface: A remark that the name Heather is another girl's name, which looks like stating the obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the Latin genus name for heath plants, and it is also a common female forename.

clue.text: This regularly beats free newspaper – getting little chap to appear topless!

indicators.note: without a top means the first letter of the little chap is removed

blocks.note: Metro is a free daily newspaper handed out on British public transport
a gnome is a small man of folklore

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline: a free paper outdoes rivals by getting a little man to pose topless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beats' looks like defeats, but the definition describes a device that ticks out time; GNOME loses its G.
explanation.definitionFit: A metronome is the device musicians use to keep tempo, ticking at a steady regular pulse.

clue.text: Sign on railway showing place to find books

blocks.note: Libra is a sign of the zodiac
RY is an abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A sign on a railway platform points the way to a bookshop or reading room.
explanation.definitionFit: A library is a building or room where a collection of books is kept for reading or borrowing.

clue.text: Passed some inside spa, leisurely heading back

indicators.note: only part of the run of letters is wanted, so the answer sits within the words
going back means the concealed letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of inside, all of spa and the start of leisurely

explanation.surface: Time slips by in a spa while someone strolls back at a leisurely pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' looks like a container signal but is part of the letter string; DESPALE read backwards is ELAPSED.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that has elapsed has passed or gone by, so the two past-tense verbs match.

clue.text: Really scared if I'd messed about with Peter

indicators.note: things messed about with are jumbled up, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone admits they would be terrified if they had dared to tamper with Peter.
explanation.definitionFit: To be petrified is to be frozen with fear, an intensified synonym for very frightened.

clue.text: A six-footer giving instructions? It may be an impossible demand

blocks.note: first meaning, whimsical: a lanky person who issues commands
second meaning: a request that is unreasonably hard to fulfil

explanation.surface: A towering person barking orders is pictured as making unreasonable demands.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the first meaning as a pun on the two words read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall order is an idiom for a task or request that is very difficult to meet.

clue.text: I mend tiny breaks in security

indicators.note: something that breaks falls into pieces, which are then rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A repairer boasts of fixing small breaches in a security system.
explanation.definitionFit: An indemnity is protection or insurance against loss, a form of financial security.

clue.text: More than one of these heard when toasting happiness?

definitions.text: More than one of these heard when toasting
definitions.note: the toast is the plural, so this defines the singular

blocks.clueFragment: More than one of these heard when toasting
blocks.note: first meaning: the plural of this word is what people say as they raise their glasses
second meaning: gladness or good spirits

explanation.surface: A question about what is heard at a toast, and whether it signals happiness.
explanation.walkthrough: Drinkers clink glasses and say the plural form, so one of them is the singular noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheer as a noun means gaiety or good spirits, as in good cheer, a synonym for happiness.

clue.text: Severely criticize players having one way to enter

blocks.note: the cast are the actors in a production
the Roman numeral for one
a gate is an entrance

explanation.surface: Critics slate a company of actors who have just one entrance on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: To castigate is to reprimand or rebuke harshly, a formal synonym for criticizing severely.

clue.text: Leads to trouble in parts of Yorkshire?

indicators.note: putting something to trouble disturbs it, so the letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about whether certain clues or guides cause trouble somewhere in Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: The Yorkshire Dales are a hilly national park in northern England; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Dales are valleys, and the Yorkshire Dales are the best-known upland region in that county.

clue.text: Salesman by apartment returning smartly dressed

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the combined letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: a rep is a sales representative
pad is slang for a flat or home

explanation.surface: A travelling salesman comes back to his flat looking smart.
explanation.definitionFit: Dapper describes a neat, trim man who is smartly turned out.

clue.text: Middle of comic's bad quips, sadly unimpressive thing

indicators.note: the centre of the word comic is all that is kept
things that go sadly go wrong, so the letters are put in a fresh order

blocks.note: the central letter of comic
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A comedian's poor jokes fall flat, which is sadly underwhelming.
explanation.walkthrough: A squib is a small firework; a damp one fizzles out instead of banging.
explanation.definitionFit: A damp squib is an idiom for an event that fails to live up to expectations, a letdown.

clue.text: Left in seat, shrink back

indicators.note: in places one letter within the word for a seat

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
a bench is a long seat

explanation.surface: Someone abandoned on a bench recoils in fright.
explanation.definitionFit: To blench is to flinch or recoil in fear, the same as shrinking back.

clue.text: Ballet, oddly, in concert? It's difficult to manage

indicators.note: oddly keeps only the letters in odd-numbered positions of ballet
in places the kept letters within the word for a concert

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters of ballet
a prom is a promenade concert, as at the BBC Proms in London

explanation.surface: A ballet staged within a concert proves a logistical headache.
explanation.definitionFit: A problem is a matter or situation hard to deal with or resolve, which fits a thing difficult to manage.

clue.text: Liberal owns a place in Tibet

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal
to own something is to have it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician holds property in the Himalayas.
explanation.definitionFit: Lhasa is the capital city of Tibet, so it is one example of a place there.

clue.text: A police officer with mostly tough question for "Fatty"

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter of the tough question is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
Detective Inspector, a British police rank
a poser is a puzzling question

explanation.surface: An officer puts a hard question to a suspect nicknamed Fatty.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around Fatty make it look like a nickname; here it is simply the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Adipose is a technical adjective meaning made of or relating to fat, as in adipose tissue.

clue.text: Park official losing head in rage

indicators.note: losing its head means the first letter of the official is dropped

blocks.note: a park ranger looks after a national park

explanation.surface: A furious park warden flies off the handle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing head' suggests losing one's temper, but it removes the R of RANGER.
explanation.definitionFit: Anger is strong displeasure, and rage is its most intense form, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Celtic lettering unearthed in bog hamlet

indicators.note: something unearthed has been dug out from within, so the answer lies buried in the words

blocks.note: the letters span the end of bog and the start of hamlet

explanation.surface: An archaeologist finds ancient Celtic inscriptions in a boggy village.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogham is the early medieval Irish alphabet of strokes carved on standing stones.

clue.text: Complete item of jewellery: centre's missing – charming!

indicators.note: the middle letter of the item of jewellery is taken away

blocks.note: to end something is to complete or finish it
an ornament worn on the ear

explanation.surface: Someone admires a finished piece of jewellery with a hole in the middle as delightful.
explanation.walkthrough: EARRING has seven letters, so its centre is the fourth, the second R.
explanation.definitionFit: Something endearing inspires affection, so it is close in sense to charming or winning.

clue.text: When required, a hospital doctor comes round

indicators.note: coming round something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: taken as written
doc is informal for doctor
H is the map and sign abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A hospital doctor visits a patient whenever needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes round' suggests a doctor's ward round, but it signals DOC going round H.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad hoc is Latin for for this purpose, describing something arranged only as and when it is needed.

clue.text: Tedious, being back in outskirts of Derby

indicators.note: the outskirts of a town are its edges, so only the outermost letters are kept
in places one piece inside the edges of the city name

blocks.note: first and last letters of Derby
the rear is the back of something

explanation.surface: Life on the edge of Derby, an English city, is said to be boring.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreary means dull and depressing, a close synonym for tedious or wearisome.

clue.text: Cold and damp, but spacious, by the sound of it

indicators.note: judging by the sound means a word is wanted that is pronounced like another

blocks.note: roomy means having plenty of space

explanation.surface: A house is described as chilly and damp but at least it is big.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheumy describes air or weather that is raw and damp, likely to bring on rheum or catarrh.
